title: Harbor Fresh Seafood: borrow or lease a truck, time value of money and the balance sheet
participant_role: Financial accountant advising HARBOR FRESH SEAFOOD

difficulty.rationale: A loan schedule plus an annuity and single-amount present value comparison with a residual value is solid ICDC work; lease accounting is kept to one qualitative point so it fits 10 minutes.

scenario:
You are to assume the role of financial accountant for HARBOR FRESH SEAFOOD, a wholesale seafood distributor that delivers fresh fish to restaurants and grocery stores. The owner (judge) needs a new $100,000 refrigerated delivery truck and has asked you to compare two ways of paying for it.

Option A is to buy the truck with a bank loan: a 5-year, 6% note payable for $100,000. The loan requires equal annual principal payments of $20,000 plus interest on the unpaid balance, paid at the end of each year. The truck is expected to be worth $20,000 at the end of the 5 years.

Option B is to lease the truck for 5 years, with payments of $23,000 at the end of each year. The truck would be returned to the leasing company at the end of the lease.

The owner (judge) prefers the lease. The owner says, "The lease payment is lower, and leasing keeps the debt off our balance sheet so the bank will not worry about how much we owe." The owner has also been reading that interest rates may rise next year and is unsure what that means for the decision.

[Loan terms, lease terms and present value factors: see exhibits]

You must:
- Prepare the payment schedule for the bank loan
- Calculate and compare the present value cost of buying the truck with the loan and of leasing it
- Explain how each option would appear on the balance sheet
- Explain how rising interest rates could affect the decision and recommend the better option for Harbor Fresh Seafood

You will present your analysis to the owner (judge) in a role-play to take place in the owner's office. The owner (judge) will begin the role-play by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented your analysis and have answered the owner's (judge's) questions, the owner (judge) will conclude the role-play by thanking you for your work.

judge_questions: Why does the truck's value after 5 years matter so much?
If the Fed raises rates next year, does my fixed 6% loan change?

solution.overview: A strong answer completes the loan schedule ($18,000 total interest, $118,000 total paid), values the lease at $96,885, and compares it with the net present value cost of buying ($100,000 minus the $14,946 present value of the $20,000 residual, or $85,054), so buying is about $11,831 cheaper. The student corrects the owner: under current U.S. GAAP the lease also appears on the balance sheet, so it does not hide the debt. The student then explains how rising rates affect loans, leases and present values and recommends buying.

answer: Interest = 6% x unpaid balance: 6,000, 4,800, 3,600, 2,400, 1,200
Total payments fall from $26,000 in Year 1 to $21,200 in Year 5
Total interest $18,000; total paid $118,000
After Year 1: note balance $80,000, current portion $20,000, long-term portion $60,000
Lease payments are an ordinary annuity: PV = 23,000 x 4.2124 = $96,885 (total cash 5 x 23,000 = $115,000)
PV of the loan payments at 6% equals the $100,000 borrowed
Buying also gives a truck worth $20,000 later: PV = 20,000 x 0.7473 = $14,946, so net PV cost to buy = $85,054
Buying is about $11,831 cheaper if the residual estimate holds
Compare present values, not total cash paid ($118,000 vs $115,000), because the payments happen at different times
Loan: truck recorded at cost $100,000 as equipment and a note payable of $100,000
Truck is depreciated, for example (100,000 minus 20,000) / 5 = $16,000 per year straight-line
Under current U.S. GAAP a lease of this kind is also reported on the balance sheet (a right-of-use asset and a lease liability of about $96,885), so leasing does not keep the debt off the books
Both liabilities are split into current and long-term portions, so the bank sees the obligation either way
A fixed 6% loan does not change; a variable-rate loan or any new borrowing would cost more
New lease quotes and new loans would both become more expensive, so locking in a fixed rate now is valuable
Higher discount rates lower the present value of future payments
Recommend buying with the fixed-rate 6% loan: about $11,831 cheaper in present value and Harbor Fresh owns the truck
Plan for the higher early payments in the cash budget ($26,000 in Year 1 vs $23,000); lease only if flexibility or maintenance coverage is worth more than the extra cost

Buy versus lease
calculations.result: Buying is about $11,831 cheaper in present value terms

judge_question_answers.question: Why does the truck's value after 5 years matter so much?
answer: Only the owner keeps the truck; a lessee returns it
The $20,000 residual is worth 20,000 x 0.7473 = $14,946 today, and it is what makes buying cheaper
Without it, buying costs $100,000 in present value versus $96,885 to lease, so leasing would be $3,115 cheaper
Buying wins as long as the truck is worth more than about 3,115 / 0.7473 = $4,168 after 5 years, so the estimate should be checked against used truck prices

judge_question_answers.question: If the Fed raises rates next year, does my fixed 6% loan change?
answer: No, a fixed-rate note keeps its 6% rate and payment schedule for all 5 years
Only variable-rate debt or new borrowing would cost more
Rising rates actually make the locked-in 6% loan more valuable to Harbor Fresh

key_concepts.definition: A dollar today is worth more than a dollar in the future because it can earn interest.
Today's value of a single future amount. PV = future amount x PV factor (for example 20,000 x 0.7473).
A series of equal payments made at the end of each period. PV = payment x PV annuity factor (for example 23,000 x 4.2124).
A written promise to repay borrowed money with interest; the part due within one year is a current liability, the rest is long-term.
Interest = principal still owed x annual rate, so interest falls as principal is repaid.
The asset a lessee reports under current U.S. GAAP for its right to use a leased item; recorded at the present value of the lease payments.
The lessee's obligation to make lease payments, measured at their present value; each payment covers interest first, then reduces the liability.
The expected value of an asset at the end of its useful life or the financing period; an owner keeps it, a lessee does not.
Spreading the cost of a long-term asset over its useful life. Annual depreciation = (cost minus residual value) / useful life.
A fixed rate stays the same for the life of the loan; a variable rate changes when market rates change.

notes: ICDC level because the student must combine a loan amortization schedule, annuity and single-amount present values and a residual value adjustment into one decision. Lease accounting is limited to explaining that the lease also appears on the balance sheet; no lease entries are required. Common mistakes: agreeing that the lease is off balance sheet, comparing total cash paid ($118,000 vs $115,000) instead of present values, and forgetting the $20,000 residual value belongs only to the buyer.

criteria.exceeds: Completes the loan schedule (interest of $6,000, $4,800, $3,600, $2,400 and $1,200; payments falling from $26,000 to $21,200; $18,000 total interest and $118,000 total paid), records the Year 1 payment (debit Notes Payable $20,000, debit Interest Expense $6,000, credit Cash $26,000), and splits the $80,000 balance into $20,000 current and $60,000 long-term.
criteria.meets: Completes the schedule with interest at 6% of the unpaid balance, totaling $18,000 of interest and $118,000 paid, and records the Year 1 payment correctly.
criteria.below: Calculates interest on the original $100,000 every year, or completes only part of the schedule or the entries.
criteria.little: Does not prepare the loan schedule, or the amounts are unrelated to the loan terms.

items.label: Calculate the time value of money

criteria.exceeds: Values the lease at $96,885 ($23,000 x 4.2124), the residual at $14,946 ($20,000 x 0.7473) for a net buying cost of $85,054, shows buying is about $11,831 cheaper, and explains why present values, not total cash ($118,000 versus $115,000), must be compared.
criteria.meets: Calculates the lease present value of $96,885 and the net present value cost of buying of $85,054, and concludes buying is about $11,831 cheaper.
criteria.below: Compares total cash paid ($118,000 versus $115,000) instead of present values, or forgets the $20,000 residual value belongs to the buyer.
criteria.little: Does not calculate any present values, or uses the wrong factors.

items.label: Describe the methods used to value long-term assets

criteria.exceeds: Explains the truck is recorded at its $100,000 cost with a $100,000 note payable and depreciated $16,000 a year straight-line (($100,000 minus $20,000) / 5), and corrects the owner that under current U.S. GAAP the lease also appears as a right-of-use asset and lease liability of about $96,885.
criteria.meets: States the purchased truck is recorded at cost and depreciated, and that the lease is also reported on the balance sheet, so leasing does not keep the debt off the books.
criteria.below: Describes the purchase correctly but agrees that the lease stays off the balance sheet, or cannot explain depreciation.
criteria.little: Does not explain how either option is reported, or confirms the owner's belief that leasing hides the debt.

items.label: Explain the economic impact of interest-rate fluctuations

criteria.exceeds: Explains that the fixed 6% loan does not change while new loans, lease quotes and variable-rate debt would cost more, that higher discount rates lower present values, and that locking in a fixed rate now makes buying even more attractive.
criteria.meets: Explains that a fixed 6% loan keeps its rate if rates rise, while new borrowing and new leases would become more expensive.
criteria.below: Says rising rates matter but cannot explain how they affect a fixed-rate loan versus new borrowing.
criteria.little: Does not address interest rates, or says the fixed 6% loan payment will increase.

criteria.exceeds: Delivers an organized presentation that walks the owner from the loan schedule to the present value comparison and a clear recommendation to buy with the fixed 6% loan, noting the higher $26,000 Year 1 payment must fit the cash budget.
criteria.meets: Presents the schedule, present value comparison, balance sheet effects and recommendation in a clear, logical order.
criteria.below: Presentation is disorganized, skips parts of the analysis, or ends without a clear recommendation.
criteria.little: Presentation is unclear or does not address the owner's decision.

items.label: Critical Thinking: Reason effectively and use systems thinking

criteria.exceeds: Connects timing of payments, the residual value, balance sheet reporting and interest rates into one decision, showing the lower lease payment does not make leasing cheaper.
criteria.meets: Reasons correctly from the exhibit data to the conclusion that buying costs less in present value.
criteria.below: Reaches a conclusion without showing the reasoning, or accepts the owner's view that the lower payment is cheaper.

items.label: Problem Solving: Make judgments and decisions and solve problems

criteria.exceeds: Recommends buying with the fixed-rate loan (about $11,831 cheaper) and explains when leasing could still make sense, such as if flexibility or maintenance coverage is worth more than the extra cost.
criteria.meets: Makes a clear recommendation to buy the truck with the 6% bank loan.
criteria.below: Hesitates, or gives a recommendation that is partly correct or not clearly stated.
criteria.little: Makes no recommendation, or recommends leasing because the payment is lower.

criteria.exceeds: Explains present value and lease accounting in plain language the owner can follow, and politely corrects the owner's belief about off balance sheet debt.
criteria.meets: Presents the numbers and recommendation clearly and in an organized way.
criteria.below: Presentation is hard to follow, relies on jargon, or skips steps.

items.label: Creativity and Innovation: Show evidence of creativity

criteria.exceeds: Uses a side by side comparison ($96,885 lease versus $85,054 buy) or a completed schedule that makes the decision obvious, and adds a useful idea such as checking the $20,000 estimate against used truck prices.
criteria.meets: Organizes the information in a way that makes the comparison easy to understand.
criteria.below: Presents the facts with little effort to make them engaging or easy to follow.
criteria.little: Shows no evidence of creativity or original thought.

items.label: Overall impression and responses to the judge's questions

criteria.exceeds: Answers both questions confidently: the $20,000 residual (worth $14,946 today) is what makes buying cheaper, since without it leasing would be $3,115 cheaper and buying wins only if the truck is worth more than about $4,168; and a fixed 6% note does not change if the Fed raises rates, which makes it more valuable.
criteria.meets: Answers both questions mostly correctly, including that only the owner keeps the residual value and that the fixed 6% loan does not change.
criteria.below: Answers only one question correctly, or gives vague answers without numbers.
criteria.little: Cannot answer the judge's questions, or says the fixed loan rate will rise.

Year 1 entry: debit Notes Payable $20,000, debit Interest Expense $6,000, credit Cash $26,000
Net present value cost of buying = $100,000 minus ($20,000 x 0.7473 = $14,946) = $85,054, so buying is about $11,831 cheaper
Compare present values, not total cash paid ($118,000 versus $115,000)
Under current U.S. GAAP the lease is also on the balance sheet (right-of-use asset and lease liability of about $96,885)
A fixed 6% loan does not change if rates rise; new borrowing and leases would cost more
Recommend buying with the fixed-rate loan and planning for the $26,000 Year 1 payment
